rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In this warning to the avaricious, opening graves also evokes treasures buried after usurping God's and people's rights.
rows.anchor: These verses sound a warning to people who are ungrateful and

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb for what happens to the hearts means separating and splitting a collected thing for inspection, so nothing remains concealed.
rows.anchor: means to separate and split something which is collected in order to inspect it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Secrets within hearts are gathered too, so each person is shown evidence of the motives behind every deed.
rows.anchor: secrets buried in the hearts of men will also be gathered so that

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wrongdoers invent respectable motives to quiet conscience and avoid censure; especially religious pretenders and leaders can disguise their inner selves.
rows.anchor: whatever evil a person perpetrates, he wants to legalize it by trying

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People will see not only their deed records but also their motives; readers should consult the end of al-Zilzāl for related aspects.
rows.anchor: S ūrah al-Zilz āl, the previous sūrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God already knows deeds and motives, but wisdom prevents their full disclosure now; Judgment Day reveals each record and lets others see God's knowledge of inner and outer selves.
rows.anchor: The Almighty is aware of the deeds and motives of all people

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says God would make His Prophet forget whatever He willed.
rows.anchor: قال كان الله ينسي نبيه صلى الله عليه وسلم ما يشاء

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda identifies the panting runners as horses that pant while running.
rows.anchor: قال هي الخيل حتى تضبح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghuthāʾ, with light or doubled thāʾ, is debris a flood casts to a valley edge, including grass, plants, and rags; an unnamed poet uses it of flood debris.
rows.anchor: الغثاء، مخفف الثاء ومشددها: ما يقذف به السيل على جانب الوادي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥawāʾ is blackness tinged with green; Dhū al-Rumma's line uses it of a woman's lip.
rows.anchor: الحوة: سواد يضرب إلى الخضرة، قال ذو الرمة:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view makes ḥawāʾ green overlaid with black; al-aḥwāʾ may also be a gazelle with black and white back stripes, illustrated by an unnamed poet.
rows.anchor: وقيل: خضرة عليها سواد، والأحوى: الظبي الذي في ظهره خطان

rows.speaker: الأعلم
rows.claim: Al-Aʿlam describes ḥawāʾ as a color tending toward black, including intense green tending toward black.
rows.anchor: وقال الأعلم: لون يضرب إلى السواد، وقال أيضا: الشديد الخضرة

rows.speaker: الصحاح
rows.claim: Al-Ṣiḥāḥ glosses ḥawāʾ as brown.
rows.anchor: وفي الصحاح: الحوة: سمرة، وقال الأعلم:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūra is Meccan; its opening answers who created the human mentioned in the previous sūra.
rows.anchor: هذه السورة مكية. ولما ذكر فيما قبلها فلينظر الإنسان مم خلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding sūra called revelation decisive speech, and this sūra identifies it with God's promise to recite it to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: إنه لقول فصل ، قيل: هو سنقرئك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sabbih means declaring God free of defects; the apparent reading directs glorification to God's name, excluding its use for idols, which even more strongly entails God's transcendence.
rows.anchor: سبح: نزه عن النقائص، اسم ربك: الظاهر أن التنزيه يقع على الاسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some take the name to mean the named one; another view says God's name should only be mentioned reverently.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الاسم هنا بمعنى المسمى. وقيل: معناه نزه اسم الله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās interprets the command as praying in the name of the Most High Lord, with a preposition omitted.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: المعنى صل باسم ربك الأعلى، كما تقول: ابدأ

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet directed worshippers to say the Most High Lord's glorification in prostration, following the direction for the Great Lord in bowing.
rows.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: «اجعلوها في ركوعكم»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Aʿlā can modify Lord in genitive or name in accusative; the latter fails if alladhī khalaq is an adjective of Lord because another adjective intervenes.
rows.anchor: الأعلى يصح أن يكون صفة لربك، وأن يكون صفة لاسم فيكون منصوبا،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If alladhī khalaq is instead a predicate of an omitted subject or an accusative of praise, al-Aʿlā can modify the name.
rows.anchor: فإن لم يجعل الذي صفة لربك، بل ترفعه على أنه خبر مبتدأ محذوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God created everything and proportioned it without disparity, with fitting harmony and precision that indicate a knowing, wise creator.
rows.anchor: الذي خلق: أي كل شيء، فسوى: أي لم يأت متفاوتا بل متناسبا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority read qaddara with doubled dāl, allowing meanings of decree or measured proportion.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: قدر بشد الدال، فاحتمل أن يكون من القدر والقضاء،

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says God assigned each animal what suits it, guided it to that provision, and taught it how to benefit from it.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: قدر لكل حيوان ما يصلحه، فهداه إليه

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī reads qaddara with a light dāl, deriving it from power or measurement and proportion.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الكسائي: قدر مخفف الدال من القدرة أو من التقدير

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says the mention of guidance suffices while its opposite, leading astray, is left implicit.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: فهدى وأضل، اكتفى بالواحدة عن الأخرى.

rows.speaker: الكلبي ومقاتل
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī and Muqātil say God guided animals to mate.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي ومقاتل: هدى الحيوان إلى وطء الذكور للإناث.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says humans are guided to good and evil, while livestock are guided to grazing grounds.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: هدى الإنسان للخير والشر، والبهائم للمراتع.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view is that a newborn is guided to suckle; the cited accounts are examples, not exclusive interpretations.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هدى المولود عند وضعه إلى مص الثدي، وهذه الأقوال محمولة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent syntax makes aḥwā an adjective of ghuthāʾ; Ibn ʿAbbās explains blackness as old flood debris that rots after rain.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن أحوى صفة لغثاء. قال ابن عباس: المعنى فجعله غثاء أحوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading makes aḥwā a circumstantial description of pasture, dark from intense, well-watered greenness; its delay preserves the verse endings.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أحوى حال من المرعى، أي أحرى المرعى أحوى، أي للسواد من شدة خضرته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A cited verse describes rainfall and greenness, continuing the discussion of pasture's dark green color.
rows.anchor: وغيث من الوسمي حوتلاعه ... تبطنته بشيظم صلتان

rows.speaker: الحسن وقتادة ومالك
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, and Mālik take the promise as meaning the Prophet should not move his tongue hastily while revelation is coming.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن وقتادة ومالك: هذا في معنى لا تحرك به لسانك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God promises to recite revelation and preserve it for the unlettered Prophet, making this a sign of prophethood.
rows.anchor: وعده الله أن يقرئه، وأخبره أنه لا ينسى، وهذه آية للرسول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative takes the promise as recitation of the sūras and the negative as emphatic reassurance; it then warns against neglecting regular review.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هذا وعد بإقراء السور، وأمر أن لا ينسى على معنى التثبيت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alif remains in falā tansā despite the jussive prohibition particle, to regularize the verse endings.
rows.anchor: وأثبتت الألف في فلا تنسى، وإن كان مجزوما بلا التي للنهي لتعديل رؤوس الآي.

rows.speaker: الحسن وقتادة وغيرهما
rows.claim: They take the exception as what God decreed to abrogate, removing both its recitation and ruling.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن وقتادة وغيرهما: مما قضى الله نسخه، وأن ترتفع تلاوته وحكمه.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says God may make the Prophet forget something so that he can establish it as a practice.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: إلا ما شاء الله أن ينسيك لتسن به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view allows temporary forgetting followed by a reminder, as when the Prophet said ʿAbbād's recitation reminded him of verses in a sūra.
rows.anchor: كما قال عليه الصلاة والسلام، حين سمع قراءة عباد بن بشير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further view interprets not forgetting as not abandoning practice, except where God abrogates the ruling.
rows.anchor: فلا تنسى: أي فلا تترك العمل به إلا ما شاء الله أن تتركه

rows.speaker: الفراء وجماعة
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ and others treat the exception as a conventional formula, with nothing actually exempted.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء وجماعة: هذا استثناء صلة في الكلام على سنة الله تعالى

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī adopts that view: the exception denies forgetting altogether, using rare phrasing without intending a real exception.
rows.anchor: والغرض نفي النسيان رأسا، كما يقول الرجل لصاحبه: أنت سهيمي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects the empty-exception account as making God's exception no exception at all, unsuitable even in eloquent speech.
rows.anchor: وهذا لا ينبغي أن يكون في كلام الله تعالى، بل ولا في كلام فصيح.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He also rejects the weak proposal that lā is prohibitive and the alif remains only for rhyme.
rows.anchor: وكذلك القول بأن لا في فلا تنسى للنهي، والألف ثابتة لأجل الفاصلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clear sense is that the Prophet will not forget except through abrogation, forgetting to establish a practice, or temporary forgetting followed by recall; he is protected from forgetting what he must convey.
rows.anchor: والمعنى أنه تعالى أخبر أنه سيقرئه، وأنه لا ينسى إلا ما شاء الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise follows the command to glorify because glorification requires reciting revelation; it allays the Prophet's fear of forgetting while reserving forgetfulness for a divine purpose.
rows.anchor: لما أمره تعالى بالتسبيح، وكان التسبيح لا يتم إلا بقراءة ما أنزل عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God knows the Prophet's audible Qur'an recitation and his private fear that it might escape him, and has relieved that fear by promising to recite it.
rows.anchor: جهرك بالقرآن، وما يخفى: أي في نفسك من خوف التفلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause about making the Prophet's way easy is coordinated with the recitation promise; the intervening assurance is parenthetical, and ease first means retaining revelation.
rows.anchor: ونيسرك معطوف على سنقرئك، وما بينهما من الجملة المؤكدة اعتراض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other interpretations make the easy way the lenient Ḥanīfī law or good worldly and afterlife outcomes, including victory, high rank, and Paradise.
rows.anchor: وقيل: للشريعة الحنيفية السهلة. وقيل: يذهب بك إلى الأمور الحسنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After promising recitation and ease, God commands reminder because recitation should benefit the Prophet and those to whom he was sent.
rows.anchor: ولما أخبر أنه يقرئه وييسره، أمره بالتذكير، إذ ثمرة الإقراء هي انتفاعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The condition if reminder benefits is a rebuke to Quraysh, implying that the defiant will not benefit.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الأمر بالتذكير مشروط بنفع الذكرى، وهذا الشرط إنما جيء به توبيخا لقريش

rows.speaker: الفراء والنحاس والزهراوي والجرجاني
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ, al-Naḥḥās, al-Zahrawī, and al-Jurjānī interpret the condition as even if the reminder does not benefit.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء والنحاس والزهراوي والجرجاني معناه: وإن لم ينفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation makes in mean when, as in the statement that believers are superior when they believe.
rows.anchor: إن بمعنى إذ، كقوله: وأنتم الأعلون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only the fearful take heed: fear prompts reflection on escape, and reflection leads to truth; these include scholars and believers in differing measure.
rows.anchor: سيذكر من يخشى: أي لا يتذكر بذكراك إلا من يخاف، فإن الخوف حامل على النظر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The feminine object that the most wretched avoid is the reminder; the most wretched are those who disbelieve in the Messenger.
rows.anchor: هؤلاء هم العلماء والمؤمنون كل على قدر ما وفق له. يتجنبها

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says the greatest fire is the fire of the afterlife, while the lesser fire is that of this world.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: النار الكبرى: نار الآخرة، والصغرى: نار الدنيا.

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ identifies the greatest fire as the lowest of Hell's levels.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: الكبرى: السفلى من أطباق النار.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says afterlife fires differ in intensity, with some greater than others.
rows.anchor: وقيل: نار الآخرة تتفاضل، ففيها شيء أكبر من شيء.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The damned neither die to rest nor live pleasantly; thumma signals the added severity of remaining between life and death after burning.
rows.anchor: ثم لا يموت: فيستريح، ولا يحيى حياة هنيئة وجيء بثم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aḥlaḥa means to win and obtain one's desire, and tazakkā means to purify oneself.
rows.anchor: قد أفلح: أي فاز وظفر بالبغية، من تزكى: تطهر.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās interprets purification as leaving associationism and professing there is no god but God.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: من الشرك، وقال: لا إله إلا الله.

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan takes purification to mean that a person's deeds are sound and pure.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: من كان عمله زاكيا.

rows.speaker: أبو الأحوص وقتادة وجماعة
rows.claim: Abū al-Aḥwaṣ, Qatāda, and others say the person gives some wealth and purifies it.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو الأحوص وقتادة وجماعة: من رضخ من ماله وزكاه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Remembering the Lord's name means affirming His oneness; prayer includes obligatory worship and whatever supererogatory worship one can manage.
rows.anchor: وذكر اسم ربه: أي وحده، لم يقرنه بشيء من الأنداد، فصلى: أي أتى الصلاة المفروضة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage describes a person who remembers, believes, and succeeds through prayer and almsgiving.
rows.anchor: والمعنى: أنه لما تذكر آمن بالله، ثم أخبر عنه تعالى أنه أفلح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He calls weak the argument that the verse proves the opening takbīr is obligatory, may use any divine name, and lies outside prayer because prayer is conjoined to it.
rows.anchor: واحتج بقوله: وذكر اسم ربه على وجوب تكبيرة الافتتاح

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says remembering the Lord's name means remembering the return and standing before Him, then praying to Him.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: وذكر اسم ربه: أي معاده وموقفه بين يدي ربه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority read tuʾthirūna as direct address to the unbelievers; another view addresses both righteous and wicked, who prefer the world for different reasons.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: بل تؤثرون بتاء الخطاب للكفار. وقيل: خطاب للبر والفاجر

rows.speaker: عبد الله وأبو رجاء والحسن والجحدري وأبو حيوة وابن أبي عبلة وأبو عمرو والزعفراني وابن مقسم
rows.claim: These readers pronounce yuʾthirūna in the third person rather than addressing the audience.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله وأبو رجاء والحسن والجحدري وأبو حيوة وابن أبي عبلة وأبو عمرو

rows.speaker: ابن زيد وابن جرير
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd and Ibn Jarīr say this refers to the report that those who purify succeed while people prefer worldly life; Abū Ḥayyān favors this for proximity.
rows.anchor: قاله ابن زيد وابن جرير، ويرجح بقرب المشار إليه بهذا.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وعكرمة والسدي
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, and al-Suddī take this as referring to the sūra's meanings.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس وعكرمة والسدي: إلى معاني السورة.

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says this refers to the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك: إلى القرآن.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says this points specifically to the statement that the afterlife is better and more lasting.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: إلى قوله: والآخرة خير وأبقى.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ʿādiyāt describes swift runners, while exegetes dispute what is running; ḍabḥ is a loud sound during strenuous running, distinct from ordinary animal calls.
rows.anchor: العاديات: الجاريات بسرعة، وهو وصف، ويأتي في التفسير الخلاف في الموصوف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās is quoted as saying only horses and dogs pant, but Abū Ḥayyān doubts this attribution because Arabic applies ḍabḥ to many animals and even a bow.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس: ليس يضبح من الحيوان غير الخيل والكلاب. قيل: ولا يصح

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abū Ḥanīfa's verse about a bow uses ḍabḥ for the bow's sound, likened to a fox.
rows.anchor: أنشد أبو حنيفة في صفة قوس: حنانة من نشم أو تألب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word may originally describe a fox and be transferred to horses; it is linked to fire changing a color without fully burning it, or a slight darkening.
rows.anchor: وقال أهل اللغة: أصله للثعلب، فاستعير للخيل، وهو من ضبحته النار

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda equates ḍabḥ and ḍabʿ with running very fast.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: الضبح والضبع بمعنى العدو الشديد

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad derives ḍabḥ from the horse's quick gait.
rows.anchor: وكذا قال المبرد: الضبح من إضباعها في السير.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qadḥ can mean striking or extracting; the eye's removal of impurities and the tools for striking sparks illustrate its range.
rows.anchor: القدح: الصك، وقيل: الاستخراج، ومنه قدحت العين: أخرجت منها الفاسد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aghāra means attacking an enemy to plunder, kill, or capture.
rows.anchor: أغار على العدو: قصده لنهب أو قتل أو أسر.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naqʿ means dust; two poetic citations use it for dust raised in battle.
rows.anchor: النقع: الغبار. قال الشاعر: يخرجن من مستطار النقع دامية

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda also glosses naqʿ as raising one's voice, citing Labīd.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: النقع: رفع الصوت، ومنه قول لبيد:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kanūd means ungrateful for a blessing; an unnamed poet applies it to someone ungrateful for men's generosity.
rows.anchor: الكنود: الكفور للنعمة، قال الشاعر: كنود لنعماء الرجال

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās gives dialectal senses: disobedient in Kinda and Ḥaḍramawt, ungrateful in Rabīʿa and Muḍar, and miserly with poor management in Kināna.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس: الكنود، بلسان كندة وحضر موت: العاصي

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil identifies the Kināna dialect sense as a miser with bad stewardship.
rows.anchor: وبلسان كنانة: البخيل السيء الملكة، وقاله مقاتل.

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī gives the same dialect account except that he assigns the miserly sense to Banū Mālik and omits Ḥaḍramawt.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي مثله إلا أنه قال: وبلسان بني مالك: البخيل

rows.speaker: أبو زبيد
rows.claim: Abū Zubayd's line uses kanūd of a miserly age or fate, continuing the lexical evidence for the word.
rows.anchor: إن تفتني فلم أطب عنك نفسا ... غير أني أمنى بدهر كنود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥaṣala can mean to collect, distinguish from something else, or become manifest and clear.
rows.anchor: حصل الشيء: جمعه، وقيل: ميزه من غيره،

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود وجابر والحسن وعكرمة وعطاء
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd, Jābir, al-Ḥasan, ʿIkrima, and ʿAṭāʾ classify the sūra as Meccan.
rows.anchor: هذه السورة مكية في قول ابن مسعود وجابر والحسن وعكرمة وعطاء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وأنس وقتادة
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Anas, and Qatāda classify the sūra as Medinan.
rows.anchor: مدنية في قول ابن عباس وأنس وقتادة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding sūra threatened Judgment Day and rebuked those who fail to prepare for it and prefer worldly matters to the afterlife.
rows.anchor: لما ذكر فيما قبلها ما يقتضي تهديدا ووعيدا بيوم القيامة

rows.speaker: الجمهور من أهل التفسير واللغة
rows.claim: The majority of exegetes and linguists identify the runners as horses racing in God's way and panting as they run; ʿAntara's verse illustrates their panting.
rows.anchor: والجمهور من أهل التفسير واللغة على أن العاديات هنا الخيل، تعدو في سبيل الله

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله وعلي وإبراهيم والسدي ومحمد بن كعب وعبيد بن عمير
rows.claim: These authorities identify the runners as pilgrims' camels charging from ʿArafāt and Muzdalifa during pilgrimage.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبد الله وعلي وإبراهيم والسدي ومحمد بن كعب وعبيد بن عمير: العاديات: الإبل

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: ʿAlī argued for camels by citing Badr, where the Muslims had only two horses, and Ibn ʿAbbās then returned to his interpretation.
rows.anchor: وبهذا حج علي رضي الله عنه ابن عباس حين تماريا

rows.speaker: صفية بنت عبد المطلب
rows.claim: Ṣafiyya bt. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib's verse depicts the pilgrims' runners at Jamʿ raising dust.
rows.anchor: وقالت صفية بنت عبد المطلب: فلا والعاديات غداة جمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍabḥan is parsed as an omitted cognate verb, a circumstantial expression, or—following Abū ʿUbayda's gloss of running—as a cognate accusative.
rows.anchor: وانتصب ضبحا على إضمار فعل، أي يضبحن ضبحا أو على أنه في موضع الحال

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī allows ḍabḥan to modify al-ʿādiyāt as if the phrase meant panting runners; Abū Ḥayyān objects that panting and running are not identical.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: أو بالعاديات كأنه قيل: والضابحات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mūriyāt describes sparks produced when the horses' hooves strike stones against one another; this spark is called the fire of al-Ḥabāḥib.
rows.anchor: والإيراء: إخراج النار، أي تقدح بحوافرها الحجارة فيتطاير منها النار

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: An unnamed poet's line describes the fire of al-Ḥabāḥib sparked by striking stones.
rows.anchor: وتوقد بالصفاح نار الحباحب

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda reads the sparking as metaphor: the horses ignite war; Abū Ḥayyān links this image to God's extinguishing war's fires.
rows.anchor: وقيل: فالموريات قدحا مجاز، أو استعارة في الخيل تشعل الحرب، قاله قتادة.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وزيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and Zayd b. Aslam say the sparking ones are a group plotting against someone, as in the idiom I will kindle against you.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس ومجاهد وزيد بن أسلم: الموريات: الجماعة التي تمكر في الحرب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās also says the image refers to people lighting night fires for their needs and food.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس أيضا: التي توري نارها بالليل لحاجتها وطعامها.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report from Ibn ʿAbbās identifies a raiding party whose numerous fires frighten the enemy.
rows.anchor: وعنه أيضا: جماعة الغزاة تكثر النار إرهابا.

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima says men's tongues kindle a fire through forceful speech, proofs, and arguments that reveal truth and defeat falsehood.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة: ألسنة الرجال توري النار من عظيم ما تتكلم به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The raiders attack the enemy at dawn; for camel interpreters the word can mean running fast from Muzdalifa to Mina or at Badr.
rows.anchor: فالمغيرات صبحا: أي تغير على العدو في الصبح، ومن قال هي الإبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fāʾ conjunctions imply succession, supporting one entity through all these descriptions; Abū Ḥayyān prefers horses used in fighting unbelieving enemies.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا دليل على أن هذه الأوصاف لذات واحدة، لعطفها بالفاء التي تقتضي التعقيب.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Badr's having only two horses does not establish the camel reading: the sūra is not said to have been revealed because of Badr, and camels are not the normal mounts of jihad.
rows.anchor: ولا يستدل على أنها الإبل بوقعة بدر، وإن لم يكن فيها إلا فرسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fa-atharna coordinates with the active participle as a verb in meaning: the runners ran, raided, then raised dust.
rows.anchor: وتقول أصحابنا: هو معطوف على الاسم، لأنه في معنى الفعل.

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī instead says the clause coordinates with the verb replaced by the active participle.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: معطوف على الفعل الذي وضع اسم الفاعل موضعه

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most readers lighten both thāʾ in atharna and sīn in wasaṭna; some double both, while ʿAlī, Zayd b. ʿAlī, Qatāda, and Ibn Laylā double only sīn.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: فأثرن، فوسطن، بتخفيف الثاء والسين

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says doubled atharna means they revealed dust or proposes a word reversal; Abū Ḥayyān calls the reversal contrived.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: وقرأ أبو حيوة: فأثرن بالتشديد، بمعنى: فأظهرن به غبارا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains doubled wasaṭna as causative and the preposition as added for emphasis; Abū Ḥayyān says both forms are reported with the same sense.
rows.anchor: وقرىء: فوسطن بالتشديد للتعدية، والباء مزيدة للتوكيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in the first phrase refers to dawn; in the second it may refer to dawn or to dust, so the horses entered among the group in the dust.
rows.anchor: قيل: أو على النقع، أي وسطن النقع الجمع، فيكون وسطه بمعنى توسطه.

rows.speaker: علي وعبد الله
rows.claim: ʿAlī and ʿAbd Allāh say the phrase describes camels reaching Jamʿ, the proper name for Muzdalifa, rather than a group of people.
rows.anchor: وقال علي وعبد الله: فوسطن به جمعا: أي الإبل

rows.speaker: بشر بن أبي حازم
rows.claim: Bishr b. Abī Ḥāzim's verse uses Jamʿ for a people and depicts a survivor escaping the dust.
rows.anchor: وقال بشر بن أبي حازم: فوسطن جمعهم وأفلت حاجب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other readings refer the pronoun to the charge implied by al-ʿādiyāt or to a place understood from context though not mentioned.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الضمير في به معا يعود على العدو الدال عليه والعاديات أيضا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation understands naqʿ here as shouting.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المراد بالنقع هنا الصياح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath is by the generic class of runners, not a previously identified group, and its answer is that man is ungrateful to his Lord.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن المقسم به هو جنس العاديات، وليست أل فيه للعهد

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A prophetic report describes the kanūd as one who eats alone, withholds help, and beats his servant.
rows.anchor: وفي الحديث: «الكنود يأكل وحده ويمنع رفده

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan define kanūd as denying God's blessings.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس والحسن: هو الجحود لنعمة الله تعالى.

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan also describes the kanūd as one who counts wrongs against his Lord and forgets good deeds.
rows.anchor: وعن الحسن أيضا: هو اللائم لربه، يعد السيئات وينسى الحسنات.

rows.speaker: الفضيل
rows.claim: Al-Fuḍayl says the kanūd lets one sin erase many good deeds from memory and treats God as a transaction partner.
rows.anchor: وقال الفضيل: هو الذي تنسيه سيئة واحدة حسنات كثيرة، ويعامل الله على عقد عوض.

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ says the kanūd withholds help from his people in calamities.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء: هو الذي لا يعطي في النائبات مع قومه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation defines kanūd as miserly; Ibn Qutayba uses barren land that grows nothing as a lexical analogy.
rows.anchor: وقيل: البخيل. وقال ابن قتيبة: أرض كنود: لا تنبت شيئا.

rows.speaker: الحسن ومحمد بن كعب
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Muḥammad b. Kaʿb take the witness to be the human being, who cannot deny his ingratitude because it is evident.
rows.anchor: والظاهر عود الضمير في وإنه على ذلك لشهيد، أي يشهد على كنوده

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda instead make the pronoun refer to God, whose witnessing is a threat.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس وقتادة: هو عائد على الله تعالى، أي وربه شاهد عليه

rows.speaker: التبريزي
rows.claim: Al-Tabrīzī also identifies God as witness and calls that the sounder view because the pronoun returns to the nearest antecedent.
rows.anchor: وقال التبريزي: هو عائد على الله تعالى، وربه شاهد عليه هو الأصح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān rejects proximity alone as decisive and prefers consistent pronouns with a single referent when the sense permits.
rows.anchor: ولا يترجح بالقرب إلا إذا تساويا من حيث المعنى. والإنسان هنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The human is strongly attached to good, meaning wealth; shadīd means intense in love, though it may instead mean tightfisted and controlling of wealth.
rows.anchor: وإنه: أي وإن الإنسان، لحب الخير: أي المال، لشديد: أي قوي في حبه.

rows.speaker: طرفة
rows.claim: Ṭarafa's line uses al-mutashaddid for a person who tightly hoards wealth.
rows.anchor: وقال طرفة: أرى الموت يعتام الكرام ويصطفي ... عقيلة مال الفاحش المتشدد

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says that wherever khayr occurs in the Qur'an it means wealth.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: الخير من حيث وقع في القرآن هو المال.

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya allows worldly goods such as wealth, health, and favor with rulers; ignorant unbelievers know no other good, whereas love of afterlife's good is praiseworthy.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يراد هذا الخير الدنيوي من مال وصحة وجاءه عند الملوك

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says the syntax means intense love of wealth, with the final word for love omitted because it has already appeared and to preserve the verse ending.
rows.anchor: فلما تقدم الحب قال لشديد، وحذف من آخره ذكر الحب لأنه قد جرى ذكره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another analysis treats the lām as causal: because of love of wealth the person is miserly or intensely attached to it, while weak in worship and gratitude.
rows.anchor: بل اللام في لحب لام العلة، أي وإنه لأجل حب المال لبخيل

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī glosses shadīd as closed and constricted rather than openhanded toward goods.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: أو أراد: وإنه لحب الخيرات غير هش منبسط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question warns people to consider their end; yaʿlam has an omitted object, roughly whether one knows one's destination when the graves are overturned.
rows.anchor: أفلا يعلم: توقيف إلى ما يؤول إليه الإنسان، ومفعول يعلم محذوف

rows.speaker: الحوفي
rows.claim: Al-Ḥūfī parses idhā as an adverb governed by yaʿlam; Abū Ḥayyān says this is unclear because the meaning is whether one knows now.
rows.anchor: وقال الحوفي: إذا ظرف مضاف إلى بعثر والعامل فيه يعلم. انتهى، وليس بمتضح

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read buʿthira passively with ʿayn; ʿAbd Allāh reads it with ḥāʾ, al-Aswad b. Zayd reads baḥatha, and Naḍr b. ʿĀṣim reads baḥthara actively.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: بعثر بالعين مبنيا للمفعول. وقرأ عبد الله: بالحاء.

rows.speaker: ابن يعمر ونصر بن عاصم ومحمد بن أبي سعدان
rows.claim: Ibn Yaʿmar, Naṣr b. ʿĀṣim, and Muḥammad b. Abī Saʿdān read ḥuṣṣila actively, while the majority read it passively.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن يعمر ونصر بن عاصم ومحمد بن أبي سعدان: وحصل مبنيا للفاعل

rows.speaker: ابن يعمر ونصر بن عاصم
rows.claim: Ibn Yaʿmar and Naṣr b. ʿĀṣim also read with light ṣād; this means the contents of the breasts are assembled and revealed, or distinguished and uncovered for recompense.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن يعمر أيضا ونصر بن عاصم أيضا: وحصل مبنيا للفاعل خفيف الصاد

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read inna with kasra and the lām in la-khabīr, treating the verse as an independent report; God is always knowing but will recompense them on that day.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: إن بكسر الهمزة، لخبير باللام: هو استئناف إخبار

rows.speaker: أبو السمال والحجاج
rows.claim: Abū al-Sammāl and al-Ḥajjāj read inna with fatḥa and omit the lām, allowing yaʿlam to govern the clause; the commentary discusses the resulting syntactic difficulty.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو السمال والحجاج: بفتح الهمزة وإسقاط اللام.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is the Prophet's special divine guidance after the general guidance given to creatures: receiving and preserving the Qur'an and being enabled to guide humanity.
rows.anchor: سنقرئك فلا تنسى بيان لهدايته تعالى شأنه الخاصة برسوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sīn may be emphatic or promise continued revelation, with recitation now and of future revelation; God is said to recite by metonymy through Gabriel, its intermediary.
rows.anchor: والسين إما للتأكيد وإما لأن المراد اقراء ما أوحي إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet will not forget because of his strong retention despite being unlettered; this itself is a sign, alongside the Qur'an's inimitability and reports of unseen events.
rows.anchor: فلا تنسى أصلا من قوة الحفظ والأتقان مع أنك أمي لم تكن تدري

rows.speaker: جعفر الصادق
rows.claim: Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq is cited for an alternative that the Prophet could read writing but could not write, becoming a reader by inspiration without instruction.
rows.anchor: فقد روي عن جعفر الصادق رضي الله تعالى عنه أنه عليه الصلاة والسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He says the inspired-reader interpretation conflicts with transmitted early explanations and with the causal fāʾ.
rows.anchor: وفيه أنه مع كونه خلاف المأثور عن السلف في الآية تأباه فاء التفريع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative construes not forgetting as not neglecting the Qur'an's commands, a promise of compliance that al-Ālūsī regards as far-fetched.
rows.anchor: وجوز أيضا أن يكون المراد نفي نسيان المضمون أي سنقرئك القرآن فلا تغفل عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reading falā tansā as a prohibition with a retained alif for rhyme is strained because forgetting is involuntary; appeals to figurative neglect or orthography also require contortions.
rows.anchor: وقيل فلا تنسى نهي والألف لمراعاة الفاصلة كما في قوله تعالى وأضلونا السبيلا

rows.speaker: الإمام المرزوقي
rows.claim: Al-Marzūqī is cited as saying that when an alif is lengthened at pause, a deleted alif is restored.
rows.anchor: مع أن الإمام المرزوقي صرح بأنه عند الإطلاق ترد المحذوفة

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority identify al-ʿādiyāt as horses of raiders running swiftly for God's cause; the word derives from al-ʿādawāt with wāw changed to yāʾ after a kasra.
rows.anchor: والعاديات الجمهور على أنه قسم بخيل الغزاة في سبيل الله تعالى التي تعدو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍabḥan is a verbal noun with an omitted verb and a circumstantial clause; it is the horses' breathing sound while running.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى ضبحا مصدر بفعله المحذوف أي تضبح أو يضبحن ضبحا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says horses make an ah-ah sound when running; ʿAlī says panting is a horse's ḥamḥama and a camel's breathing.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن جرير وابن المنذر عن ابن عباس الخيل إذا عدت قالت أح أح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary describes ḍabḥ as a loud sound during strenuous running, neither whinnying, growling, nor barking; it doubts Ibn ʿAbbās's restriction to horses and dogs.
rows.anchor: في البحر تصويت جهير عند العدو الشديد ليس بصهيل ولا رغاء ولا نباح

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abū Ḥanīfa's bow verse applies ḍabḥ to a bow's fox-like sound, supporting broader Arabic usage.
rows.anchor: أنشد أبو حنيفة في صفتها حنانة من نشم أو تالب

rows.speaker: عنترة
rows.claim: ʿAntara's verse applies panting to horses running in the waters of death.
rows.anchor: كما في قول عنترة والخيل تكدح حين تضبح في حياض الموت ضبحا

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda equates ḍabḥ and ḍabʿ with running very fast, allowing ḍabḥan to function as a cognate accusative or a circumstantial expression.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة الضبح وكذا الضبع بمعنى العدو الشديد

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority identify al-Qāriʿa as the Resurrection itself, from the first blast to the judgment between creatures.
rows.anchor: الجمهور على انها القيامة نفسها ومبدوها النفخة الاولى ومنتهاها فصل القضاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other interpretations identify al-Qāriʿa as the sound of the blast or, according to al-Ḍaḥḥāk, the fire with rage and roaring; the commentary rejects al-Ḍaḥḥāk's view.
rows.anchor: وقيل صوت النفخة وقال الضحاك هي النار ذات التغيظ والزفير وليس بشيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whatever its referent, al-Qāriʿa comes from striking forcefully enough to produce a loud sound.
rows.anchor: وأياما كان فهي من القرع وهو الضرب بشدة بحيث يحصل منه صوت شديد

rows.speaker: عيسى
rows.claim: ʿĪsā reads al-Qāriʿa in the accusative, supplying an omitted imperative: remember the catastrophe.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عيسى القارعة بالنصب وخرج على أنه باضمار فعل أى اذكر القارعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God will teach the Prophet through Gabriel's recitation.
rows.anchor: سنقرئك} سنعلمك بقراءة جبريل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception means what God wills the Prophet to forget, including Qur'anic recitation whose abrogation is a kind of making one forget.
rows.anchor: أن تنساه، وما نسخ الله تلاوته من القرآن

rows.speaker: مجاهد والكلبي
rows.claim: Mujāhid and al-Kalbī report that the Prophet used to begin reciting a verse before Gabriel finished it, fearing he would forget; after this reassurance he forgot nothing.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد، والكلبي: كان النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم إذا نزل عليه جبريل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God knows what people make public in speech and action and what they conceal; in other words, He knows secret and open matters.
rows.anchor: والمعنى: أنه يعلم السر والعلانية.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وعطاء ومجاهد وعكرمة والحسن والكلبي وقتادة والمقاتلان وأبو العالية
rows.claim: These authorities identify al-ʿādiyāt as horses running in God's cause; ḍabḥ is the sound from their bodies while running.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس، وعطاء ومجاهد، وعكرمة، والحسن، والكلبي، وقتادة، والمقاتلان

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says horses, dogs, and foxes pant when exhausted or frightened; the word relates to fire changing a color.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: وليس شيء من الحيوانات تضبح غير الفرس والكلب والثعلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍabḥan is parsed as a cognate accusative, equivalent to saying the running horses pant.
rows.anchor: نصب على المصدر، مجازه: والعاديات تضبح ضبحا

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: ʿAlī identifies al-ʿādiyāt as pilgrims' camels traveling from ʿArafāt to Muzdalifa and then Mina, and invokes Badr's two-horse force against the horse reading.
rows.anchor: وقال علي: هي الإبل في الحج، تعدو من عرفة إلى المزدلفة، ومن المزدلفة إلى منى

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود ومحمد بن كعب والسدي
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd, Muḥammad b. Kaʿb, and al-Suddī also adopt the camel interpretation.
rows.anchor: وإلى هذا ذهب ابن مسعود، ومحمد بن كعب، والسدي.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some camel interpreters explain ḍabḥan as the camels stretching their necks while moving.
rows.anchor: يعني ضباحا تمد أعناقها في السير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-marʿā is the growth animals graze on.
rows.anchor: أخرج المرعى } أنبت ما ترعاه الدواب.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After becoming green, the pasture is made dry and black; alternatively, aḥwā describes pasture made black by intense greenness.
rows.anchor: بعد خضرته. { غثاء أحوى } يابسا أسود.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise may mean reciting the Qur'an through Gabriel or inspiring the Prophet to become a reader.
rows.anchor: على لسان جبريل عليه الصلاة والسلام، أو سنجعلك قارئا بإلهام القراءة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet will not forget because of strong memory despite illiteracy; the prediction's fulfillment is another sign of his prophethood.
rows.anchor: أصلا من قوة الحفظ مع أنك أمي ليكون ذلك آية أخرى لك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view treats falā tansā as prohibition, with the alif retained for rhyme as in the cited form al-sabīlā.
rows.anchor: وقيل نهي والألف للفاصلة كقوله تعالى السبيلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception may refer to forgetting through abrogation of recitation; alternatively, it may signal rarity, and a report says the Prophet forgot a verse during prayer.
rows.anchor: نسيانه بأن نسخ تلاوته، وقيل أراد به القلة والنذرة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The known and hidden may mean people's outward and inward states, or the Prophet's public recitation with Gabriel and his private fear; God knows what preservation or forgetting benefits them.
rows.anchor: ما ظهر من أحوالكم وما بطن، أو جهرك بالقراءة مع جبريل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūra's Meccan or Medinan status is disputed, and it has eleven verses.
rows.anchor: مختلف فيها، وآيها إحدى عشرة آية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath is by horses of raiders whose panting is their breath during running; ḍabḥan can be an omitted verb's object, cognate accusative, or circumstantial adjective.
rows.anchor: أقسم سبحانه بخيل الغزاة تعدو فتضبح ضبحا، وهو صوت أنفاسها عند العدو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mūriyāt means those that bring out sparks; īrāʾ is producing fire, as when flint is struck and sparks appear.
rows.anchor: فالتي توري النار، والإيراء إخراج النار يقال قدح الزند فأورى.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The raiders attack the enemy in the morning.
rows.anchor: يغير أهلها على العدو. { صبحا } أي في وقته.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Atharna means they stirred up dust or shouting, by that time.
rows.anchor: فهيجن. { به } بذلك الوقت. { نقعا } غبارا أو صياحا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wasaṭna means they entered among enemy groups in that time, in the charge, or in the dust.
rows.anchor: فتوسطن بذلك الوقت أو بالعدو، أو بالنقع أي ملتبسات به. { جمعا }

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet sent out cavalry, received no news for months, and then the sūra was revealed.
rows.anchor: روي: أنه عليه الصلاة والسلام بعث خيلا فمضت أشهر لم يأته منهم خبر فنزلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A possible allegory makes the runners souls, the sparks lights of knowledge kindled by thought, the raid an assault on desires and customs, and the dust yearning among the exalted.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون القسم بالنفوس العادية أثر كما لهن الموريات بأفكارهن أنوار المعارف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Meccan sūra, commonly placed fourteenth in revelation after al-ʿAṣr, centers on the Last Day and opens with a sudden, rapid raid that throws its victims into confusion.
rows.anchor: السورة مكية، والمشهور أنها الرابعة عشرة في ترتيبالنزول، نزلت بعد سورة العصر.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The image after the oath recalls familiar dawn raids; the following image shifts to the unseen but certain Resurrection, which suddenly leaves people disoriented and graves disgorge them like scattered moths.
rows.anchor: ثم تأتي بعدها صورة أخرى لغيب غير مشهود، ولكنه واقع حتما: البعث يفجأ على غير موعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The secrets of hearts are assembled with nothing hidden escaping; the vivid scene confirms resurrection and warns of exact, difficult reckoning.
rows.anchor: قد حصل، لم تفلت منه خافية مضمرة، مطوية في أعماق الصدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The usual oath reading treats the wāw as magnifying and emphasizing its object, which drives far-fetched interpretations.
rows.anchor: الواو في أصل الاستعمال اللغوي للقسم، ويتجه به جمهور المفسرين إلى تعظيم ما يقسم به

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن
rows.claim: Many commentators, including Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan, identify the runners as horses and restrict them to Muslim horses at Badr to explain the oath's honorific force.
rows.anchor: فهي الخيل فيما ذهب كثير منهم، ولكي يستقيم لهم مفهوم بالقسم بها، تأولوها بخيول المسلمين

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: In Ibn ʿAbbās's report, ʿAlī challenges the horse reading because Badr was Islam's first battle and Muslims had only al-Zubayr's and al-Miqdād's horses; he says the runners are camels from ʿArafāt.
rows.anchor: والله إن كانت لأول غزوة في الإسلام بدر، وما كان معنا إلا فرسان

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The reported camel interpretation describes pilgrims racing from ʿArafāt through Muzdalifa toward Mina and raising dust at Wādī Muḥassir.
rows.anchor: العاديات ضبخاً، الإبل من عرفة

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: ʿAbd Allāh b. Masʿūd also interprets the runners as camels, a view followed by other commentators who emphasize the pilgrims' dignity.
rows.anchor: إلى تفسيرها بالإبل، وتابعه على هذا عدد من المفسرين

rows.speaker: أصحاب التأويل بالخيل
rows.claim: Horse interpreters argue that the next verse's sparks must come from horseshoes, since camel hooves are too soft to spark, as al-Jurjānī says.
rows.anchor: إذ لا يكون الإيراء، وهو قدح الشرر، إلا لسنابك الخيل.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The absence of Muslim jihad and raiding horses at Mecca does not disprove the horse reading, since God could swear by a familiar feature of horses.
rows.anchor: فهذا لا يلزم، لأنه سبحانه أقسم بما يعرفونه من شأن الخيل

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب القرظي
rows.claim: Muḥammad b. Kaʿb al-Quraẓī makes the sparkers pilgrims lighting fires at Muzdalifa, requiring an implied word for groups; Ibn al-Qayyim calls this remote and says the sparkers are the runners and raiders.
rows.anchor: فقال محمد بن كعب، القرظى: هم الحاج أوقدوا نيرانهم ليلة المزدلفة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: If the report from ʿAlī is authentic, al-Zamakhsharī says panting has been borrowed for camels as bodily terms are borrowed for humans.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: "إن صح ما روى عن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dispute remains unresolved, and Bint al-Shāṭiʾ attributes it to both sides' assumption that the oath must magnify its object, restricting the animals to warhorses or pilgrims' camels.
rows.anchor: وهكذا يظل الخلاف دون أن ينحسم. فلكل قول رد، ولكل إعتراض جواب!

rows.speaker: ابن القيم
rows.claim: Ibn al-Qayyim says the horses need not be limited to raiders; the oath honors the noble animal through which people gain strength, victory, and vengeance on enemies.
rows.anchor: فالقسم إنما وقع بما تضمنه شأن هذه العاديات من خلق هذا الحيوان

rows.speaker: محمد عبده
rows.claim: Muḥammad ʿAbduh expands the horse interpretation as encouragement to value, acquire, train, and ride horses, prepare for defense, and excel in horsemanship.
rows.anchor: لينوه بشأنها، ويعلى من قدرها في نفوس المؤمنين أهل العمل والجد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As argued in her commentary on al-Ḍuḥā, the oath's wāw is more likely to have moved beyond its literal oath function for a rhetorical purpose.
rows.anchor: وقد مضى القول، في تفسير سورة الضحى، بأن القسم بالواو هنا أقرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūra's atmosphere does not praise horses or urge their acquisition and racing; it presents a sudden raid, with short verses and rapid transitions from running to sparks, dust, and penetration of the group.
rows.anchor: وإنما هو مشهد مثير، لغارة مفاجئة تصبح القوم بغتة على غير إنتظار.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ʿādiyāt occurs only here in the Qur'an; the root conveys distance and exceeding, reflected in swift running beyond ordinary pace, enmity's distance, and transgression beyond right.
rows.anchor: الأصل اللغوي للعدو هو البعد والتجاوز، ومنه العدوة للمكان المتباعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though horsemen can be called al-ʿādiyāt, ḍabḥ identifies horses themselves because it is their breathing sound when they run fast.
rows.anchor: وقد يقال للفرسان عادية، لكن الضبح يعين أن المقصود بها هنا الخيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍabḥan may be a cognate accusative with an omitted verb or a circumstantial adjective; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ prefers the verbal noun for its absolute, unrestricted sense.
rows.anchor: لما فيها من معنى الإطلاق المحض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fāʾ linking mūriyāt to al-ʿādiyāt suggests causation: sparks result from hard running as the horses' hooves strike stones.
rows.anchor: وعطف الموريات قدحا على العاديات ضبحا، بالفاء وفيها ملحظ السببية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root qadḥ occurs in the Qur'an only here; īrāʾ also appears in 56:71 in its basic sense of kindling fire.
rows.anchor: ولم ترد مادة قدح في القرآن إلا في هذه الآية، أما الإيراء فجاء فعلا مضارعا

rows.speaker: أصحاب الإبل
rows.claim: Camel interpreters cite 56:71 to construe mūriyāt as pilgrims kindling fires at Muzdalifa; Ibn al-Qayyim calls this a remote interpretation and says the sparkers are the runners.
rows.anchor: استشهد الذين قالوا إن العاديات هي إبل الحاج، ففسروا الموريات بأنها جماعات الحجيج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fāʾ conveys cause and immediate succession without delay from the horses' running to their dawn attack.
rows.anchor: والعطف بالفاء، فيه مع ملحظ من السببية، ترتيب دون تراخ أو تمهل وإبطاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic associates a raid with horses even when they are not named; to raid is to unleash horses, and a horse raids by accelerating, supporting this interpretation.
rows.anchor: العربية تخص الإغارة بالخيل، ولو لم يذكر لفظ الخيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dawn specifies surprise because the enemy is unprepared and unaware; al-Tibyān and Muḥammad ʿAbduh make the same point.
rows.anchor: أما تخصيص الإغارة بوت الصبح فلم يفت المفسرين إدراك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic uses morning as a raid day, and Qur'anic morning, dawn, and early-day language often signals surprise and warning, as in cited destruction passages.
rows.anchor: أن اللغة استعملت يوم الصبح بمعنى يوم الغارة، وأن القرآن الكريم استعمل الصباح والإصباح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Further examples of morning surprise and warning include the destruction passages at 54:38, 7:78, and 11:81, alongside the other listed verses.
rows.anchor: وأنظر معها آيات: الكهف 41، 42، القلم 21

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fāʾ connects raising dust to the dawn raid with immediate succession, matching the scene's speed.
rows.anchor: بالفاء أيضا، ربطت آية: {فَأَثَرْنَ بِهِ نَقْعًا}

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī asks what fa-atharna coordinates with and says it follows the verb represented by the participle, meaning those that ran, sparked, and raised dust; Muḥammad ʿAbduh offers a similar analysis.
rows.anchor: وللزمخشري هنا وقفتان: الأولى عند الفعل {أَثَرْنَ} علام عطف

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī refers the pronoun in bihi to dawn, meaning the horses raised dust at that time; this is also found in the Juzʾ ʿAmma commentary.
rows.anchor: فأرجعه الزمخشري إنما إلى الصبح، أي أثرن بذلك الوقت نقعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bint al-Shāṭiʾ prefers taking the pronoun as referring to the preceding raid, sparks, and running, understood from context.
rows.anchor: فأثرن بالإغارة والقدح والعدو..... وهذا عندي أولى....

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fāʾ in wasaṭna suits the sudden, swift raid: its stages press forward continuously without pause.
rows.anchor: والعطف بالفاء هنا، ملائم لجو الموقف الذي تسيطر عليه الأخذة المباغتة
